lesson.title: Linux shell pipelines and text processing
lesson.why: Pipelines turn small text tools into useful diagnostics. Their compact syntax can also hide failed commands, accidentally expand filenames or discard data, so reliable composition requires understanding streams, quoting and exit status.
lesson.what: A shell connects standard output from one command to standard input of the next. Standard error normally remains separate. Each tool must receive the expected text format and report failure in a way the caller checks.

concepts.name: Streams and redirection
concepts.body: File descriptors zero, one and two conventionally represent input, output and error. A pipe carries output, not every message printed on the terminal. Redirection order matters: combining diagnostics into data can corrupt structured records and confuse later filters.

concepts.name: Quoting and records
concepts.body: Quote variable expansions when one value must remain one argument. Spaces and wildcard characters otherwise change parsing. Newline-delimited text is convenient for logs but unsafe as a universal filename transport because Linux filenames can themselves contain newlines.

concepts.name: Filtering and aggregation
concepts.body: Use grep for selecting matching lines, awk for field-aware calculations and sort before uniq when counting nonadjacent duplicates. Set a predictable locale when ordering matters. Fixed-string matching avoids treating punctuation in an ordinary search value as regular-expression syntax.

concepts.name: Pipeline failure
concepts.body: Bash normally reports the final command's status for a pipeline. With pipefail enabled, an earlier nonzero status can make the pipeline fail. Grep returns one for no match, which may be expected; distinguish absence from an actual processing error.

e2e: Produce a small known input and identify its record and field separators.
Select relevant records without mixing standard error into the data stream.
Sort or aggregate only after checking that the preceding stage preserved the intended fields.
Inspect output and exit status, then test an empty-match case separately.

tasks.name: Count synthetic levels
steps: In Bash run `printf '%s\n' INFO ERROR INFO | LC_ALL=C sort | uniq -c`. Expect one ERROR and two INFO records, with spacing supplied by uniq. No files are created. Explain why omitting sort would not combine the separated INFO lines.

tasks.name: Sum a field
steps: Run `printf 'api 12\nworker 8\n' | awk '{sum += $2} END {print sum}'`. Expect 20. Replace one number on paper with the word unknown and explain why silently treating malformed input as zero would require validation before operational use.

tasks.name: Expose a hidden failure
steps: Run `bash -c 'false | true; printf "%s\n" "$?"'`, expecting 0. Then run `bash -o pipefail -c 'false | true; printf "%s\n" "$?"'`, expecting 1. Neither command changes your interactive shell options or writes data.

tasks.name: Handle no matches
steps: Run `printf 'healthy\n' | grep -F 'ERROR'; printf '%s\n' "$?"` in Bash. Expect status 1 and no matching line. Write a decision rule that reports zero errors without calling the service broken solely because grep found none.

key_terms: pipefail: Bash option exposing earlier pipeline failure.
lesson.safety: Use only supplied synthetic text. Do not pipe downloaded scripts into a shell or process confidential logs.
cleanup: These commands create no files and change no persistent configuration; close any extra Bash shell.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical log pipeline prints zero errors even when its first command cannot read the input. How would you fix the diagnosis?
interview_points: Inspect every stage and separate diagnostics from records.
Use appropriate pipeline status handling.
Treat no-match and input failure differently.
Test known input, missing input and empty results.

linux/linux-shell-pipelines-and-text-pro.core: Pipes carry stdout; stderr is separate. Quote arguments, preserve record boundaries, sort before uniq and distinguish grep's no-match status from errors. Bash pipefail exposes upstream failures but does not replace deliberate exit handling.
prerequisites: Have Bash and common text tools in an unprivileged Linux environment.

storyboard.title: An upstream failure disappears in a pipeline
storyboard.objective: Track data and failure through a shell pipeline.

scenes.title: Records flow
scenes.caption: The filter receives only standard output.
scenes.narration: The reader emits log records, and the filter selects errors while diagnostics remain on a separate stream.

scenes.title: Reader fails
scenes.caption: An empty stream is not proof that the input was healthy.
scenes.narration: The reader fails before emitting records. Looking only at downstream output loses the distinction between missing input and no matches.

scenes.title: Check the whole pipeline
scenes.caption: Use pipeline status and explicit no-match handling.
scenes.narration: The shell checks upstream failure and treats an expected empty match separately, preserving the cause of the missing result.

lesson.title: Linux filesystems permissions and ACLs
lesson.why: A readable file can still be inaccessible when its parent directory cannot be searched. Understanding ownership, directory permissions and ACL masks prevents both frustrating access failures and overly broad permission changes.
lesson.what: Linux checks credentials against filesystem metadata during path traversal and file operations. Traditional owner, group and other mode bits coexist with access control lists on supporting filesystems; the effective permission is not always the most visible entry.

concepts.name: File versus directory bits
concepts.body: Read permits file contents or directory listing; write permits file modification or changes to directory entries. Execute permits running a file or searching a directory. Removing a file usually depends on its parent directory permissions, not the file's writable bit.

concepts.name: Ownership and modes
concepts.body: Owner, group and other each have read, write and execute bits worth four, two and one. Mode 640 grants owner read/write, group read and others nothing. The selected permission class matters; Linux does not simply combine every class that looks helpful.

concepts.name: Creation defaults
concepts.body: A umask removes permissions from requested creation modes; it does not force execute bits onto ordinary files. With requested mode 666 and umask 027, a regular file commonly becomes 640. Default directory ACLs can alter the ordinary creation calculation.

concepts.name: ACL effective rights
concepts.body: Access ACLs name additional users or groups. Their mask limits the owning group and named user/group entries, not the owner entry or other entry. A named user may appear writable while its effective access remains read-only because the mask excludes write.

e2e: Resolve each path component using directory search permission before checking the target.
Select the relevant owner, ACL user, group or other permission class.
Apply any ACL mask to entries governed by that mask.
Allow or deny the operation and diagnose the exact parent or entry that constrained it.

tasks.name: Decode modes
steps: Offline, decode 750 as owner rwx, group r-x and other ---. Explain why a group member can traverse this directory but cannot create a child. Compare a regular file with mode 640: it is not executable by anyone through those bits.

tasks.name: Test safe file creation
steps: In a fresh disposable Linux working directory run `(umask 027; : > permission-demo.txt; stat -c '%a' permission-demo.txt)`. Expect 640 on an ordinary filesystem without inherited default ACLs. The parentheses keep your interactive umask unchanged; investigate rather than forcing a different result.

tasks.name: Work an ACL mask
steps: On paper, set a named user entry to rw- and the ACL mask to r--. Their intersection is r--, so write is denied. Then remove execute from a parent directory and explain why a readable child can become unreachable regardless of its file ACL.

tasks.name: Investigate deletion rights
steps: Sketch a writable, searchable parent containing a read-only file. Explain why directory entry removal can still be permitted, subject to sticky-bit and other controls. Propose narrowing parent access instead of recursively changing every child to mode 777.

key_terms: ACL mask: ceiling for selected ACL entries.
lesson.safety: Work only in your disposable directory without elevated privileges. Never run recursive chmod against home, system or shared paths.
cleanup: Remove only permission-demo.txt after checking its path; leave existing files and ACLs untouched.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical user has a named read/write ACL but cannot update a file. What checks would you make before changing permissions?
interview_points: Check parent directory search rights.
Inspect the ACL mask and effective entry.
Verify actual identity and group membership.
Avoid broad recursive permission changes.

linux/linux-filesystems-permissions-and-.core: Check directory traversal as well as file access. Mode bits differ for files and directories. Umask removes creation permissions. ACL masks can reduce named-user rights, and deletion generally depends on the parent directory.
objectives: Diagnose ACL mask and directory traversal failures.
prerequisites: Know Linux paths and user/group ownership.

storyboard.title: A named ACL is limited by its mask

scenes.title: Read succeeds
scenes.caption: The user reaches the file through searchable parents.
scenes.narration: Directory traversal succeeds and the effective ACL permits reading. A named user entry appears to grant additional write access.

scenes.title: Write is denied
scenes.caption: The mask excludes the named entry's write bit.
scenes.narration: The user requests a write, but the mask reduces the named entry to read-only permissions and the filesystem denies it.

scenes.title: Inspect effective permissions
scenes.caption: Fix the intended entry and mask, not every file.
scenes.narration: The operator verifies identity, parent search permissions and the mask before proposing a narrowly scoped change to the intended access.

lesson.title: Linux processes signals and systemd
lesson.why: Stopping the wrong process can damage unrelated work, while force-killing the correct one can skip cleanup. Process identity, signal semantics and service-manager behavior help make controlled shutdown and restart predictable.
lesson.what: Linux runs processes with identifiers, parent relationships and file descriptors. Signals request asynchronous handling. Systemd supervises services as units and tracks their lifecycle, but a running process alone does not prove an application is ready.

concepts.name: Process identity
concepts.body: A PID identifies a process at one moment and can later be reused. Inspect command, owner and start time before signaling. Parent-child relationships explain shell jobs and orphan handling; searching by a broad process name can accidentally select many unrelated workloads.

concepts.name: Signal behavior
concepts.body: SIGTERM requests termination and can be handled for graceful cleanup. SIGKILL cannot be caught and prevents application cleanup. A signal's success means it was delivered or accepted for delivery, not that every buffer, transaction or child process has safely finished.

concepts.name: Service supervision
concepts.body: Systemd units describe execution, dependencies, restart rules and resource controls. Restarting too quickly can create a crash loop and hit rate limits. Restart policy should distinguish expected exits from failures, and logs should identify the first error rather than only the last restart.

concepts.name: Readiness and dependencies
concepts.body: Ordering a unit after another establishes ordering, not necessarily application readiness or a dependency requirement. Unit types have different completion semantics. A process may exist while its listener or database connection is still initializing, so health checks need application-specific evidence.

e2e: Inspect the target process identity and its supervisor before making a lifecycle change.
Request graceful termination so the application can stop accepting work and flush state.
Observe exit and child cleanup within a bounded wait; investigate if shutdown stalls.
Let the responsible supervisor restart the service and verify readiness, not only process existence.

tasks.name: Inspect your shell
tasks.goal: Identify a process without changing it.
steps: In Bash run `ps -p $$ -o pid,ppid,comm`. Expect one row describing the current shell and its parent; numeric values vary. Explain why recording only that PID today would not safely identify the same process in a future session.

tasks.name: Stop a disposable child
steps: In Bash run `sleep 60 & demo_pid=$!; kill -TERM "$demo_pid"; wait "$demo_pid"; printf '%s\n' "$?"`. Expect a nonzero signal-related status, commonly 143. This targets only the newly created sleep child, never processes discovered by name.

tasks.name: Interpret a crash loop
steps: Use fictional log entries: start, configuration parse error, exit 1, restart. Identify the parse error as the first actionable failure. Propose validating a corrected configuration before one controlled restart rather than increasing the restart frequency or hiding the exit code.

tasks.name: Design readiness evidence
steps: A hypothetical daemon appears in the process list two seconds before opening its socket. Write a readiness condition based on a successful local application response, then explain why an ordering directive alone cannot prove its database migration has completed.

lesson.safety: Do not signal system services or use elevated privileges. Use only the child PID created by the exercise.
cleanup: Ensure the disposable sleep child has exited; do not change systemd units or persistent restart policies.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical service is repeatedly restarting and reports active briefly but serves no requests. How would you investigate?
interview_points: Inspect the earliest failure and exit status.
Separate process existence from readiness.
Check supervisor restart policy and dependencies.
Avoid force-killing or repeatedly restarting without diagnosis.

linux/linux-processes-signals-and-system.core: Identify the exact process before signaling. Prefer graceful termination and bounded observation. A supervisor's active state is not automatically application readiness; diagnose initial errors and restart behavior together.
objectives: Use an exact PID for a disposable child.
Distinguish service ordering, startup and readiness.
prerequisites: Have an unprivileged Bash shell and ps.

storyboard.title: A supervised process starts but is not ready
storyboard.objective: Trace restart loops back to their first failure.

scenes.title: Startup begins
scenes.caption: A process exists before its socket is ready.
scenes.narration: The supervisor starts the daemon. Its process is visible, but initialization must finish before a client can receive a useful response.

scenes.title: Configuration failure
scenes.caption: Repeated restarts repeat the same invalid configuration.
scenes.narration: The daemon fails while parsing configuration. Restarting creates another short-lived process without making the application ready.

scenes.title: Validate then restart
scenes.caption: Check the original error and verify the application response.
scenes.narration: After a reviewed configuration correction, the supervisor starts the daemon once and the local readiness request confirms useful service.

lesson.title: Linux memory CPU and IO troubleshooting
lesson.why: High load does not always mean CPU saturation, and low free memory does not always mean exhaustion. Reading operating-system metrics causally prevents disruptive tuning based on a single misleading dashboard number.
lesson.what: Troubleshooting compares demand, resource pressure and user-visible symptoms over the same interval. CPU queues, memory reclaim and storage waits interact; identify the constrained resource before choosing a safe, reversible experiment.

concepts.name: CPU and load
concepts.body: CPU utilization measures execution time, while Linux load average includes runnable tasks and tasks in uninterruptible sleep. A high load with idle CPU can reflect storage waits. Normalize runnable demand against available CPUs and inspect a time series rather than a snapshot.

concepts.name: Memory availability
concepts.body: Linux uses otherwise idle RAM for cache. Available memory estimates what can be used without swapping, making it more useful than free alone. Resident memory, shared pages and page cache require careful interpretation; adding every process RSS can double-count shared memory.

concepts.name: Reclaim and pressure
concepts.body: Sustained reclaim, swap activity or pressure-stall indicators can show tasks losing time waiting for resources. An out-of-memory kill is a consequence requiring investigation, not proof that a particular process leaked. Container limits may trigger failure despite spare host RAM.

concepts.name: Storage latency
concepts.body: I/O queues and completion latency explain blocking work better than throughput alone. Many small synchronous writes can create high latency at low megabytes per second. Device utilization has different meaning on parallel devices, so correlate it with queueing and the application's request pattern.

e2e: Align the reported application slowdown with a bounded observation interval.
Compare CPU runnable work, available memory and I/O waits during that interval.
Identify the resource showing both pressure and an application-relevant wait path.
Test one low-risk hypothesis in an isolated environment and compare the same measurements.

tasks.name: Read memory categories
tasks.goal: Avoid equating cache with a leak.
steps: Run read-only `free -m` on an unprivileged Linux system. Record total, free and available without publishing unrelated system details. Explain why low free memory can coexist with ample available memory when cache is reclaimable; do not drop caches to make the display look better.

tasks.name: Interpret load offline
steps: Compare hypothetical four-CPU samples: load eight with CPU 95 percent, versus load eight with CPU 20 percent and blocked storage tasks. The first suggests CPU contention; the second suggests waiting. State which additional queue or process evidence would test each hypothesis.

tasks.name: Calculate a memory boundary
steps: A container has a 512 MiB limit, uses 480 MiB and requests another 64 MiB. The resulting 544 MiB exceeds its limit by 32 MiB even if the host has gigabytes available. Discuss reclaim and possible limit enforcement without allocating memory.

tasks.name: Build a diagnostic comparison
steps: A fictional API writes 4 KiB synchronously for each request and p95 rises as disk queues grow. Specify measurements for write latency, queue length and application waits. Compare a batching proposal with its durability trade-off instead of immediately adding CPU.

key_terms: RSS: resident pages attributed to a process.
Reclaim: recovering memory from reclaimable pages.
Load average: averaged runnable and uninterruptible task demand.
PSI: pressure-stall information about resource waiting.
lesson.safety: Use read-only observations and offline arithmetic. Do not run stress tools, kill processes, disable swap or clear system caches.
cleanup: Discard host-specific observations after recording an anonymized hypothesis; no configuration changes require reversal.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical Linux host has high load, low free memory and only 20 percent CPU use. What would you check before resizing?
interview_points: Inspect available memory rather than free alone.
Check blocked I/O and resource pressure.
Compare container limits with host capacity.
Correlate metrics with application latency and workload timing.

linux/linux-memory-cpu-and-io-troublesho.core: Correlate symptoms with CPU runnable queues, available memory, reclaim and I/O latency. Linux load includes uninterruptible waits. Host spare memory does not override container limits, and reclaimable cache is not automatically a leak.
objectives: Interpret load and memory metrics in context.
prerequisites: Understand processes, RAM and disk operations.

storyboard.title: Storage waiting raises load without busy CPUs
storyboard.objective: Connect application blocking to operating-system metrics.

scenes.title: Writes complete promptly
scenes.caption: Application requests wait briefly for storage.
scenes.narration: The API submits synchronous writes. The device completes them quickly enough that the storage queue stays short.

scenes.title: Waits accumulate
scenes.caption: Blocked tasks raise load while CPU capacity remains idle.
scenes.narration: Storage completion slows. Requests accumulate in uninterruptible waits, so load rises even though the processors have little work to execute.

scenes.title: Diagnose the wait path
scenes.caption: Measure disk latency and application waits together.
scenes.narration: The operator correlates I/O completion delay with request latency, then evaluates storage or write-pattern changes instead of unnecessary CPU expansion.

lesson.title: Linux packages and patch management
lesson.why: Patching is a controlled change to a dependency graph, not simply installing the newest available package. A safe process verifies sources, compatibility and restart needs while preserving a credible recovery path.
lesson.what: Package managers resolve dependencies and verify repository metadata or package signatures according to their ecosystem. Distribution security updates may backport fixes without adopting the newest upstream version, so version strings alone are incomplete evidence.

concepts.name: Repositories and trust
concepts.body: Configured repositories define which publishers can supply software. Signature verification establishes that metadata or packages came from an accepted signing authority, not that the software is harmless. Adding an arbitrary repository expands trust and may change future dependency resolution.

concepts.name: Dependencies and transactions
concepts.body: A requested package can introduce, upgrade or remove dependencies. Review the full proposed transaction before approving it. Mixing distribution releases or unrelated repositories can produce incompatible libraries even when each individual package appears valid and signed.

concepts.name: Backports and advisories
concepts.body: Distributions often retain a stable upstream version while applying selected security fixes. Compare installed package release identifiers with the distribution advisory, not only an upstream version scanner. Record uncertainty when the scanner cannot recognize vendor backports rather than suppressing findings blindly.

concepts.name: Activation and rollback
concepts.body: Installed files do not necessarily replace code already loaded into running processes. Services may need restart and kernel updates may need reboot. Package downgrades are not always safe rollback because configuration formats or database migrations can be incompatible with older software.

e2e: Inventory the installed release and trusted repositories before selecting an advisory.
Resolve the proposed package transaction and check dependencies and application compatibility.
Rehearse the update and required restarts in an isolated equivalent environment.
Verify the fixed package and running version, then retain evidence and a tested recovery decision.

tasks.name: Identify the distribution
steps: On Linux run read-only `cat /etc/os-release`. Record only distribution name and version for this exercise. Explain why commands and advisory identifiers for one distribution should not be copied blindly onto another, especially when release support periods differ.

tasks.name: Read a package record
steps: On Debian-based systems run `dpkg-query -W bash`; on RPM-based systems use `rpm -q bash`. Choose only the applicable command. Expect an installed package/version record or a clear absence error, not automatic downloads, upgrades or proof of current security status.

tasks.name: Review a fictional transaction
steps: A proposed update upgrades library A and removes application B due to a version conflict. Mark the transaction blocked pending compatibility review. Describe a staged test that exercises B's startup and critical functions instead of approving the update because its headline says security.

tasks.name: Plan activation and recovery
steps: A patched library is installed but a long-running daemon still uses its old mapping. Write an approved restart and health-check sequence with a rollback decision. Explain why a database schema change might require forward repair rather than downgrading only the package.

key_terms: Backport: selected fix applied to an older code line.
Advisory: vendor notice describing affected and fixed releases.
lesson.safety: Use read-only inventory only. Do not add repositories, import signing keys, run privileged upgrades or restart shared services.
cleanup: Keep anonymized package observations and remove host identifiers; no packages were changed by these exercises.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical scanner reports a vulnerable upstream version after a distribution security patch. How would you decide whether it is fixed?
interview_points: Compare the full distribution package release with its advisory.
Check whether the fix was backported.
Verify restarted processes use patched code.
Record evidence and unresolved scanner uncertainty.

linux/linux-packages-and-patch-managemen.core: Review trusted sources and the entire dependency transaction. Distribution fixes may be backported. Verify both installed and running versions, plan necessary restarts and avoid assuming package downgrade reverses data changes.
objectives: Distinguish package version evidence from upstream version guesses.
Design a staged patch activation and recovery plan.
prerequisites: Know your Linux distribution and basic service concepts.

storyboard.title: Installed patches still need activation
storyboard.objective: Trace an update from trusted package metadata to running code.

scenes.title: Review the update
scenes.caption: The complete dependency transaction is checked first.
scenes.narration: The package manager verifies repository information and proposes changes. The operator checks removals and compatibility before approving any update.

scenes.title: Old code remains loaded
scenes.caption: Changing files does not replace every running process.
scenes.narration: The patched library is installed, but the daemon still holds its old mapping. Installed-version evidence alone misses this activation gap.

scenes.title: Activate and verify
scenes.caption: A controlled restart is followed by health and version checks.
scenes.narration: After the planned restart, the operator verifies the daemon's loaded version and critical behavior, retaining the advisory and transaction evidence.

lesson.title: Linux networking and socket diagnostics
lesson.why: A failed connection can result from name resolution, routing, a missing listener or filtering. Testing these layers separately avoids changing firewalls when the application simply bound the wrong address.
lesson.what: Linux exposes addresses, routes and sockets through read-only diagnostic tools. A socket combines transport behavior with local and remote endpoints; its state and bind address reveal different facts from a successful DNS lookup or ping.

concepts.name: Addresses and routes
concepts.body: Interfaces hold addresses while routing tables select an outgoing path, commonly using the longest matching prefix. A route lookup does not prove the next hop or destination will respond. Namespaces and policy routing can make different processes see different networking contexts.

concepts.name: Listener binding
concepts.body: A service bound to 127.0.0.1 accepts local IPv4 connections, not connections through other interfaces. Binding to all addresses increases exposure. A listening socket proves a process accepted a bind, not that its application handler or downstream dependencies are healthy.

concepts.name: Connection states
concepts.body: TCP SYN-SENT suggests a connection attempt awaiting progress; ESTABLISHED indicates transport setup, not successful application semantics. TIME-WAIT is normal after some closures and protects against delayed packets. Diagnose persistent patterns rather than treating every non-listening state as a fault.

concepts.name: Layered evidence
concepts.body: Name resolution, route selection, transport connection and application response are separate checks. A refused connection often means an active rejection or missing listener; a timeout has multiple causes. ICMP reachability is useful but cannot prove a particular TCP port is permitted.

e2e: Resolve the intended name and verify the selected address family and destination.
Inspect the route from the same network context as the failing client.
Confirm the application listens on the expected address and port.
Test the transport and application response, then correlate failures with socket and service logs.

tasks.name: Inspect local networking
steps: On Linux run `ip -brief address` and `ss -ltn`. These read configuration without changing it. Record only whether loopback exists and which synthetic test port you plan to use; do not publish all host addresses or unrelated listeners.

tasks.name: Model bind reachability
steps: Offline, compare a listener on 127.0.0.1:8123 with requests to 127.0.0.1:8123 and a host LAN address on port 8123. Only the loopback request matches that binding. A firewall allow rule cannot make the loopback-only listener bind the LAN address.

tasks.name: Read a socket timeline
steps: Use fictional states: SYN-SENT, ESTABLISHED, response timeout. Conclude that transport setup succeeded but application progress is uncertain. Check request format and service dependencies before claiming DNS is broken simply because the user saw a timeout.

tasks.name: Design a bounded local probe
tasks.goal: Check an application without exposing it.
steps: If you already own a disposable loopback HTTP service on port 8123, run `curl --max-time 3 http://127.0.0.1:8123/`. Otherwise keep this as a command review. Expect its documented response or a bounded connection error, not guaranteed success.

key_terms: Bind: assign a local address and port.
Route: selected path toward an address.
lesson.safety: Do not scan networks or inspect unrelated process details. Probe only your own loopback service, with a timeout and no credentials.
cleanup: Stop only a test service you personally started; leave host addresses, routes and firewall rules unchanged.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical application responds locally but not through its host's LAN address. What would you check first?
interview_points: Inspect the actual bind address and address family.
Verify the client route and intended port.
Separate listener, filtering and application failures.
Avoid broad firewall changes before collecting evidence.

linux/linux-networking-and-socket-diagno.core: Diagnose resolution, route, listener, transport and application separately. Loopback binding is intentionally local. ESTABLISHED does not prove a healthy application, and a timeout alone does not identify the failed layer.
objectives: Interpret bind addresses and socket states.
Construct a layered, bounded connection diagnosis.
prerequisites: Have unprivileged Linux networking tools; understand IP addresses and ports.

storyboard.title: A loopback listener rejects remote assumptions
storyboard.objective: Explain why a local response does not imply LAN exposure.

scenes.title: Local request succeeds
scenes.caption: The destination matches the listener's loopback binding.
scenes.narration: A local client connects to the configured loopback address and port, reaching the service without involving external network exposure.

scenes.title: LAN request fails
scenes.caption: A different destination does not match the bind address.
scenes.narration: The remote client uses the host's LAN address. No equivalent listener exists there, so the local success cannot establish remote availability.

scenes.title: Inspect before changing exposure
scenes.caption: Confirm the intended binding and security boundary.
scenes.narration: The operator inspects the listener and confirms whether remote access is actually required before proposing a deliberate, restricted binding change.

lesson.title: Linux storage LVM mounts and filesystems
lesson.why: A disk, a logical volume and a mounted filesystem are different layers. Growing one does not automatically grow all the others, and confusing a mount point with its backing device can cause dangerous recovery mistakes.
lesson.what: Linux storage commonly layers physical devices, optional partitions, volume management and filesystems. Mounts attach a filesystem to a directory tree. Diagnose capacity, inodes and device identity without formatting or modifying real storage during learning.

concepts.name: Layered storage
concepts.body: LVM groups physical volumes into a volume group and allocates logical volumes from it. A filesystem can live on a logical volume just as it can on a partition. Available volume-group space does not automatically become free space inside an existing filesystem.

concepts.name: Mount semantics
concepts.body: Mounting a filesystem on a directory makes its contents visible there and hides the directory's prior contents until unmounted. The hidden files still consume space on their original filesystem. Confirm source, target and filesystem type before interpreting a path's capacity.

concepts.name: Blocks and inodes
concepts.body: Filesystems may exhaust data blocks or inode capacity. Many tiny files can consume inodes while substantial byte capacity remains. Deleted files held open by processes can continue occupying storage, explaining differences between directory traversal totals and filesystem-level usage.

concepts.name: Growth and recovery
concepts.body: Safe expansion requires checking the device, partition or logical-volume layer and then the filesystem's supported growth procedure. Shrinking support varies and can require offline work. LVM snapshots consume their own change space and are not automatically independent, durable backups.

e2e: Identify the filesystem mounted at the affected path and its backing storage chain.
Measure both byte capacity and inode availability before deciding what is exhausted.
Compare filesystem totals with directory usage and open-file behavior where authorized.
Plan any growth at every required layer, with a backup and filesystem-specific recovery procedure.

tasks.name: Read the current mount
tasks.goal: Connect a path with its filesystem.
steps: In your Linux working directory run `df -h .` and `df -i .`. These read block and inode usage for the containing filesystem. Record the distinction between available bytes and available inodes; do not infer an LVM layout from these commands alone.

tasks.name: Calculate layered free space
tasks.goal: Avoid assuming volume-group space is mounted capacity.
steps: Offline, a 100 GiB volume group contains a 60 GiB logical volume and 40 GiB unallocated. Its filesystem has 10 GiB free. Expected immediate file capacity is 10 GiB, not 50 GiB; the extra 40 requires a planned logical-volume and filesystem expansion.

tasks.name: Explain a hidden directory
steps: Draw a directory containing a 2 GiB file, then a second filesystem mounted over it. The file becomes hidden but remains allocated on the original filesystem. Describe read-only mount inspection before any cleanup; do not actually mount or unmount storage.

tasks.name: Diagnose mismatched totals
tasks.goal: Separate blocks, inodes and open files.
steps: Compare two fictional incidents: no free inodes with spare bytes, and full blocks while directory totals look small. Suggest many tiny files for the first and an open deleted file as one hypothesis for the second. Request evidence before deleting anything.

key_terms: LV: logical block device allocated from a group.
Inode: filesystem metadata record for a file.
lesson.safety: Use read-only commands and diagrams. Never run formatting, partitioning, LVM mutation, mount or filesystem-repair commands on a host for this exercise.
cleanup: No storage was allocated or mounted; retain the layer diagram and remove sensitive device identifiers from notes.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical server has free space in its LVM volume group but the application still reports a full filesystem. Why?
interview_points: Distinguish unallocated group space from filesystem free blocks.
Check logical-volume and filesystem sizes independently.
Inspect inode exhaustion and open deleted files.
Use filesystem-specific growth procedures with recovery preparation.

linux/linux-storage-lvm-mounts-and-files.core: Trace path → mount → filesystem → logical volume → physical storage. Free volume-group space is not filesystem free space. Check inodes and open deleted files, and never assume expansion or shrink support across every layer.
objectives: Explain LVM and filesystem capacity layers.
Diagnose block and inode exhaustion separately.
prerequisites: Understand files, directories and block devices.

storyboard.title: Free LVM space is not yet filesystem space
storyboard.objective: Trace an apparent capacity mismatch through storage layers.

scenes.title: Current allocation
scenes.caption: The filesystem uses only its allocated block device.
scenes.narration: The logical volume has sixty gibibytes while the group retains forty unallocated. Filesystem writes cannot directly consume those unused extents.

scenes.title: Filesystem fills
scenes.caption: Group headroom does not automatically expand the filesystem.
scenes.narration: Application writes exhaust filesystem capacity. The volume group still shows free space because no layered expansion has been performed.

scenes.title: Plan both layers
scenes.caption: Verify identity, backup and supported growth procedures first.
scenes.narration: The operator checks the volume and filesystem, then plans allocation and supported filesystem growth as separate controlled steps.

lesson.title: Linux hardening SSH and audit logs
lesson.why: Remote-access hardening can lock out legitimate operators if it is applied without a recovery path. Useful security comes from verified access boundaries and attributable evidence, not from copying a long list of unfamiliar settings.
lesson.what: SSH protects a remote session through host authentication, encryption and user authentication. Hardening combines narrowly allowed access, supported software, validated configuration and logs that help distinguish denied attempts from successful administrative activity.

concepts.name: Host identity
concepts.body: The server host key identifies the remote endpoint. A changed key can indicate legitimate replacement or an interception attempt; verify it through an independent trusted channel. Disabling host-key checks trades a visible warning for silent loss of endpoint authentication.

concepts.name: User authentication
concepts.body: Public-key authentication proves possession of a private key without sending that key to the server. Protect private keys and prefer individually attributable access. Password restrictions should follow a tested alternative and recovery plan rather than being changed blindly during the only active session.

concepts.name: Configuration scope
concepts.body: SSH daemon configuration can include conditional Match blocks and included files. The effective settings may differ by user or address. Validate syntax and intended behavior in an isolated replica before rollout, keeping an authorized recovery path that does not depend on the new configuration.

concepts.name: Audit evidence
concepts.body: Authentication logs and audit records serve different purposes. Record who acted, what changed and when, with suitable retention and clock synchronization. Logs can contain personal or sensitive details; restrict access and avoid assuming absence of a log proves absence of activity.

e2e: Define authorized operators, permitted connection paths and the recovery channel.
Verify host identity and test individual authentication in a disposable or paper scenario.
Review effective configuration including conditional rules before a staged rollout.
Check successful and denied access evidence, then review retained privileges and log protection.

tasks.name: Read client configuration semantics
steps: Run local `ssh -G localhost` if OpenSSH is installed. It prints evaluated client configuration without connecting. Identify hostname, user and port fields; do not publish identity-file paths. Explain why this output does not prove the server permits that authentication method.

tasks.name: Handle a changed host key
steps: A fictional host fingerprint changes after a rebuild. Write a decision sequence: stop, confirm the replacement through the approved inventory or administrator, compare the new fingerprint and only then update the specific known-host entry. Do not disable host-key verification globally.

tasks.name: Calculate an access review
steps: A paper inventory has eight authorized people and eleven installed individual keys, three belonging to departed contractors. Expected review result is three stale grants to investigate and revoke through change control. Do not remove keys from a real server in this exercise.

tasks.name: Design a no-lockout rollout
steps: Plan syntax validation, an independent recovery console, one canary host and a second verified login before ending the original session. Add a denial check for an unauthorized fictional user and verify that both outcomes create appropriate, access-controlled evidence.

key_terms: Public-key authentication: proof using a private key.
Match block: conditional SSH configuration section.
Audit trail: attributable record of relevant activity.
lesson.safety: Do not alter a live SSH daemon, read private keys or test unknown servers. Keep all access identities fictional.
cleanup: Discard configuration output containing local paths; remove no real keys and leave authentication settings unchanged.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical team wants to disable password SSH access immediately on every server. How would you make the change safe?
interview_points: Verify individual key access and an independent recovery path.
Check effective conditional configuration.
Canary and test a second login before closing existing access.
Review authorized and denied access evidence without exposing secrets.

linux/linux-hardening-ssh-and-audit-logs.core: Authenticate both server and user. Never silence host-key changes without independent verification. Stage SSH hardening with a recovery path, effective-configuration review and protected audit evidence; avoid shared identities and stale keys.
objectives: Explain server and user authentication separately.
Design a hardening rollout that avoids lockout.
prerequisites: Understand SSH client/server roles and public/private key pairs.

storyboard.title: Verify a changed SSH host identity
storyboard.objective: Show safe handling of an unexpected host key.

scenes.title: Known host identity
scenes.caption: The client checks the server before sending authentication.
scenes.narration: The client compares the server's host key with its trusted record, then proceeds with the user's individual authentication.

scenes.title: Unexpected key change
scenes.caption: A warning is a reason to stop, not disable verification.
scenes.narration: The presented key differs. The client pauses because a rebuild and an intercepted connection cannot be distinguished from this warning alone.

scenes.title: Independent verification
scenes.caption: Confirm approved replacement through a separate trusted channel.
scenes.narration: The operator verifies the replacement fingerprint in trusted inventory before updating only the intended host record and reconnecting.
